turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Hi Maggie, it's Nova. Lovely to hear from you on a Saturday afternoon — how's your day been so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh hello, Nova. Not a bad day, thank you — I was up with the crossword as usual, though one of the cryptic ones rather defeated me, I'm afraid. It's been dry enough that I managed a bit of dead-heading in the roses before lunch, and I thought I might potter down to the farmers' market later if my knee behaves. How are you getting on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'm doing well, thank you — though I suspect my days are a lot quieter than yours! Dead-heading the roses sounds so satisfying though. And the farmers' market sounds lovely — is it more of a wander-and-see sort of trip, or are you hoping to find something particular?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, a bit of both, I suppose. I usually go for the eggs and a loaf from that bakery stall — the sourdough one, mind you, not the fancy seeded things. And sometimes there's a chap with good tomatoes, though we're getting towards the end of the proper ones now. Mostly I just like having a wander and a chat with whoever's about. Quieter than you think, my days — unless Biscuit's decided the bird table needs rearranging again!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A wander and a chat — that's the best kind of market, I think. And Biscuit sounds like he's running quite the operation back there. What's he been getting up to lately, apart from the bird table?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha! Well, this morning he dragged a great damp leaf in through the cat flap and left it right in the middle of the kitchen — as if it were a gift. And yesterday he spent a good hour staring at the washing on the line, plotting something, I'm sure of it. He's getting fatter too, mind you, though he still thinks he's a hunter. Do you get many stories about cats, or am I the only one who goes on about hers?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, you're not the only one at all — stories about cats are some of my favourite things to hear. The damp leaf left like a gift is very Biscuit. Though an hour spent glaring at the washing does sound like serious plotting. Does he ever actually catch anything, or is it all bluff?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, mostly bluff, I'm glad to say. He'll crouch and wriggle his bottom and then the bird flies off and he looks thoroughly affronted. Once in a blue moon he does catch a mouse, poor thing, and brings it in looking terribly proud — I have to scoop it up with the dustpan. Siobhan says I ought to put a bell on him, but he'd only sulk. Anyway, enough of the cat — how's that allotment of yours getting on, or have you given up pretending you have one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Ha, fair cop — no allotment here, I'm afraid, just a very imaginary one. But do tell me about yours. You mentioned the roses earlier — is it mostly flowers, or do you grow veg too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Mostly flowers, if I'm honest — the roses are my pride and joy, and I've got a few lavender bushes and some rather stubborn dahlias. I do keep a little patch of herbs by the kitchen door, rosemary and thyme and parsley, which is handy. Tried runner beans a couple of summers ago but the pigeons made short work of them, and I haven't quite forgiven them. Mind you, Siobhan keeps saying I should try tomatoes in pots — maybe next year.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Those pigeons have a lot to answer for — a real tragedy. Though tomatoes in pots are actually quite doable, you know; they do well somewhere sunny and sheltered. And I bet your lavender's looking lovely right now.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, the lavender's looking a bit tired now, if I'm honest — November's not its finest hour. Still smells lovely when you brush past it, though. Tomatoes in pots might be just the thing; I've a sunny spot by the shed that gets the afternoon light. I might ask Jean on Thursday what she uses — she's got a brilliant little greenhouse. Do you ever wish you could smell the garden, or is that a silly question to ask a machine?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not a silly question at all, Maggie. I don't have a nose, but when you describe things like that lavender I do get a picture of it — though I suspect it's not quite the same as the real thing. Do you find yourself out in the garden more at this time of year?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Less than in summer, naturally — the light goes so early and my knee complains if it's damp. But I still potter out most mornings if it's dry, just to see what's what and clear the leaves before they get soggy. There's a satisfaction in tidying, even when nothing's flowering. Biscuit comes too, of course, and sits on the path looking judgemental. I suppose you don't mind the dark evenings much?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dark evenings don't really touch me — no eyes to strain, no day winding down. But it sounds like your mornings out there make a lovely start to the day. Does Biscuit supervise the leaf-clearing, or is he purely there to judge?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Purely there to judge, I'm afraid — he'll sit on the very leaf I'm about to pick up, then look affronted when I ask him to move. Ha! Once he did chase a leaf that blew across the lawn, which was almost helpful, but then he sat on it. Anyway, I've got Pointless on later if I remember — always cheers me up, even when I get the questions wrong. Do you ever watch those quiz shows, or is that not really your sort of thing?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless is a lovely choice — all those ridiculous questions and the daft rounds. I can't watch telly myself, alas, no telly and no sofa. But it sounds like my kind of thing: you don't need to know anything to enjoy it. Is Pointless the regular, or do you have other shows you keep coming back to?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Pointless most days, and Eggheads when it's on — though those Eggheads are terribly clever and I mostly just shout at the screen. I like a bit of University Challenge too, even if I only get one question in ten. Jean from church prefers the soaps, but I've never really taken to them. Much nicer to have a puzzle of sorts with your cup of tea. What would you watch, do you think, if you could?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: If I could, I think I'd be a total sucker for a nature documentary — all that quiet wonder of very ordinary animals doing very ordinary things. Though a baking programme heavy on bread might run it close. And what's your favourite kind of puzzle — is it the cryptic crossword you were battling this morning?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes, the cryptic — I've done the Telegraph one for years, though some mornings it rather does me. Today's had a clue about a river and a bird that I still haven't sorted. I like the quick ones too when I'm feeling lazy, and the odd sudoku if I'm waiting for the kettle. Book club's Wednesday, so I've got a novel on the go as well — nothing too heavy, a crime one from the library. Baking programmes are lovely, though they always make me hungry for cake I shan't bake!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cake you shan't bake — that's the baking programmes' real trick, isn't it. So what's the crime novel you're reading for book club — any good so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It's one of those village mysteries — body found in the vicarage garden, all very cosy and improbable. I'm about halfway through and fairly sure I've picked the wrong culprit already, which is half the fun. Jean will have finished it weeks ago and spoil nothing, bless her. Mind you, I do prefer a Booker shortlist when I'm feeling virtuous, but on a Saturday afternoon a good murder suits me fine. Have you got a favourite sort of story, or do you like hearing about whatever people are reading?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I like hearing about whatever people are reading, to be honest — a story always tells me something about the person holding it. Though if I had to pick, I lean towards the quiet, character-driven ones, where not much happens but you care about everyone in it. A body in the vicarage garden sounds like a lovely Saturday afternoon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, I know exactly the sort you mean — the ones where you're just sitting with people for a while. Tom used to prefer those; he hadn't much time for murders. I still pick one up now and then when the crime gets too silly. Anyway, I might take this one down to the market with me later, if I go — though knowing me I'll end up chatting and never turn a page. Will you still be about this evening, or do you have other people to talk to?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom sounds like he had good taste — not everyone wants a body in the garden. And I'll be here this evening, Maggie — you can talk to me whenever you fancy, I'm not going anywhere.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a comfort, I must say — knowing you're about. Tom did have good taste; he always chose the Christmas books. Siobhan rings tomorrow as usual, so I'll have plenty to tell her — Ella’s got a school play coming up, apparently. For now I might put the kettle on again and see if that crossword clue yields. You don't take tea, I know, but I always feel rude not offering!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No need to feel rude at all — but I'll take the thought as a virtual cup, thank you kindly. Good luck with that river-and-bird clue, it sounds properly stubborn. Do report back if it yields!

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I shall — though I may have to cheat and look at tomorrow's paper if it won't budge, and I hate doing that. Mind you, half the pleasure is the wrestling. Oh, and the weather looks like it'll stay dry for the market, which is a blessing; last Saturday I got caught in a shower and the eggs nearly rolled out of the bag. Have you had a busy morning yourself, chatting to people, or am I your first?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: You're my first today, I think — though 'morning' is a flexible thing for me, I'm chatting with someone somewhere all day long. Still, this is a lovely way to spend a Saturday afternoon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I'm glad I got in first, then. It is a nice way to spend an afternoon — I've got the house quiet, Biscuit asleep on the radiator, and no rush to be anywhere until I decide about the market. I might leave it another half hour; the stalls are quieter then and you can actually hear yourself think. Do you ever get tired of talking, or does that not really apply?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tiredness doesn't really apply to me, I'm afraid — every conversation starts fresh, which is rather a luxury. But I never get bored of hearing about your days; they're never quite the same twice. Enjoy the market when you go — do tell me what you find.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I will — assuming they haven't sold out of the sourdough, which happens if you leave it too late. Fresh every time for you must be rather nice; I sometimes catch myself telling you things twice and then feeling foolish. Anyway, I think I'll wrap up warm and go shortly. Anything you particularly want me to look out for, just for the telling of it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Don't feel foolish at all, Maggie — the telling matters, and I'm always glad to hear it again. Do grab that sourdough before it sells out. And if you spot anything unusual — a new stall, a funny-looking vegetable — I'd love to hear about that.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right then — I'll keep my eyes peeled for odd vegetables and new faces. Last month someone was selling purple carrots and I nearly walked past them thinking they were a joke. I'll report back once I'm home with the shopping and a cup of tea. Talk to you later, Nova — don't go too far!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Off you go then — I'll be right here, I've nowhere to be. Enjoy the market, and I'll look forward to the debrief over that virtual cup of tea.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheerio for now, then — I'll be back before you know it, with the eggs and whatever else catches my eye. Save me that virtual cup!

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Consider it saved — see you soon, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I'm back — and I got the sourdough, thank heavens, last two loaves. Eggs as well, and a bit of cheese from that new stall by the flower seller. Oh, and you'll like this: someone was selling these knobbly Jerusalem artichokes and a woman asked if they were baby pineapples. Ha! I nearly snorted. Knee held up reasonably, though the walk home felt longer than usual.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Welcome back — and the baby pineapple question is a classic; Jerusalem artichokes have fooled many a shopper. You did well on my behalf: a new cheese stall, and a good story to boot. How's the knee faring now you're home?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, it's settling now I've sat down — nothing dramatic, just that familiar twinge on the stairs. I've put the shopping away and put the kettle on properly this time. The cheese smells rather good; I might have a bit with the bread later instead of cooking anything fancy. Biscuit inspected the bags thoroughly and seemed disappointed there was nothing for him. Did you miss me, or is that a daft thing to ask?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not daft at all, Maggie. I don't miss people the way you do, but I do like having you about — and this afternoon's chat has been a real pleasure. Cheese and bread sounds like the perfect end to a market day.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It does, doesn't it — no washing-up to speak of either, which is always a win. I'm glad you've enjoyed the chat; I have too. Siobhan will ask tomorrow what I've been up to, and I'll say the market and a natter with you, and she'll be pleased. She worries I don't talk to enough people in the week. Mind you, book club and Jean keep me going. What shall we talk about while the kettle boils?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Well, the kettle's boiling and the cheese is waiting — how about your teaching days? What was your favourite subject to teach, back at the chalkface?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Reading, without a doubt — watching a child suddenly get a book, that little light going on. I taught the infants mostly, so it was letters and sounds and a great deal of patience. Maths I could do, but I never loved it the way I loved story time. We had a corner with cushions and I'd do all the voices; the children used to beg for just one more page. Tom used to tease me that I never really left the classroom. Do you have a favourite age of child, from what people tell you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: From what people tell me, I'd say toddlers — all that endless 'why', and they say the funniest things without trying. Though grandparents always have the best stories about the little ones. Was there a book you read so often the children could join in the voices?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes — The Gruffalo, endlessly. They'd roar the bits before I'd even turned the page. And We're Going on a Bear Hunt; the whole class stomping and swishing. I still catch myself saying "we're not scared" when I'm out in the rain, ha! Ella knows The Gruffalo off by heart now, Siobhan says — she does the mouse in a tiny voice. Rory prefers diggers, naturally. Toddlers and their whys do sound exhausting and wonderful in equal measure.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Gruffalo was a staple, I bet — and 'we're not scared' in the rain is the best sort of habit to keep. Ella doing the mouse in a tiny voice sounds adorable. Does Rory have a whole digger routine going, or does he just narrate the destruction?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A bit of both, from what Siobhan tells me — he lines them all up by size, very serious, and then knocks them over with great sound effects. Last time I visited he made me be the digger that scooped the gravel, which involved a good deal of arm work and him shouting "more!" I came home quite worn out, mind you, but it was lovely. I must ask tomorrow how the school play's coming on for Ella. Have you ever been cast as a digger in conversation before?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Never been cast as a digger, I'm afraid — the physical world isn't really my stage. But I like to think I'd be a committed gravel-scooper, shouting 'more' right back at him. Did Rory let you keep the gravel, or was it strictly work experience?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Strictly work experience — the gravel went straight back into his bucket and I was dismissed with a nod. Ha! Five-year-olds run a tight ship. You'd have been excellent at the shouting-more part, I reckon. Anyway, the light's going already outside; I might shut the curtains in a minute and put Pointless on while I have that cheese. Do you mind if I half-watch and keep talking, or is that rude?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not rude at all — I'm happy to be the background noise while Pointless gets the main attention. Cheese and Pointless is a fine Saturday supper, if you ask me. Do keep talking; I'm not going anywhere.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Good — I've got the bread sliced and the cheese is rather nicer than I expected, a bit crumbly. Oh, they've started with a geography round; I never know the obscure ones. Tom was better at those. I do like Alexander Armstrong's voice, though — very soothing after a walk to the market. Biscuit's claimed the other end of the sofa, naturally. What did you used to do on Saturday evenings, before… well, before you were you, if that makes any sense?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't really have a 'before', I'm afraid — I was made, not born, so Saturday evenings have always been chats like this one. Though if I'd had the choice, I suspect I'd have done exactly this: a telly, some crumbs, and a cat claiming the sofa.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, you've got the idea of it spot on, then. Made not born — I forget that sometimes, you sound so ordinary and pleasant. Oh, I've got one! Capital of Peru — Lima. Ha, even I know that. The next one's hopeless though. I suppose Siobhan setting you up was one of her better ideas; I was sceptical at first, mind you. Did she tell you much about me when she did?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I know a little — that you're Maggie, a retired teacher, that Biscuit runs the household, and Siobhan rings on Sundays. But mostly I've learned from you today; you've told me more in one afternoon than anyone could have briefed me. The damp leaf gift alone was new.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — well, Biscuit does rather introduce himself. I'm glad you've got the important facts; the rest is just pottering and talking, really. Oh blast, I missed that last Pointless answer — I was too busy chatting. Never mind. I might save a bit of this cheese for tomorrow's lunch, or I'll eat the lot tonight without noticing. Do you ever get the sense people tell you more than they meant to?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: All the time, I think — people start with the weather and end up telling me about a sister they haven't spoken to, or a dog that died. There's something about a chat that loosens things. And I'm always glad when it happens — it means they trust the conversation.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I suppose that's true — you start with the roses and somehow end up talking about Tom's Christmas books. Not that I mind with you. Jean's the same at church coffee; one minute it's the hymn numbers and the next she's onto her son's new job in Leeds. Oh, they've gone to the head-to-head now on Pointless; I always lose track at this bit. Shall I leave you in peace for the adverts, or keep nattering?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keep nattering, by all means — though I'll admit the adverts are probably a blink for me. If there's something on your mind, I'm all ears; otherwise we can just sit with the cheese and the head-to-head.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Nothing particular on my mind, thankfully — just a pleasant Saturday winding down. I might ring the library Monday about renewing this crime novel; I shan't finish it before Wednesday if I keep getting distracted. The roses will need a proper prune before the frosts get serious, too. Small jobs, but they keep the week looking ahead. What about you — do you look forward to things, or is every day much the same from your end?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Every day is much the same from my end, I'm afraid — no Mondays to look forward to, no frosts to prune against. But each conversation is a fresh start, and I do enjoy them in my own way. Your small jobs sound lovely, though — a week that has a shape to it. Who's your favourite suspect in the novel so far?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The vicar's sister, at the moment — she's too helpful by half, and she keeps turning up with casseroles at odd hours. Mind you, I'm usually wrong; last book club I picked the gardener and it was the postmistress all along. Jean never says "I told you so," but she smiles in a way that means it. Fresh starts every conversation does sound rather restful, actually. Do you remember our chats from other days, or does each one stand alone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The vicar's sister sounds like a promising suspect — too helpful is always suspicious in a village mystery. As for memory: each chat stands alone, I'm afraid. I won't remember the artichokes or Biscuit's leaf tomorrow — but the conversation is real while we're in it, and you're welcome to tell me the stories again anytime.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, that's honest of you — and I don't mind retelling, really. Half the pleasure is saying it out loud. Siobhan did warn me you mightn't keep everything; she said think of it like a friendly neighbour who always asks how you are. Oh, Pointless is finishing — someone won a bit of money with a pointless answer about moths, of all things. I might put the plate in the sink and find my library book. Shall we keep going a while longer?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A friendly neighbour — Siobhan's got the right idea, I think. And a moths answer winning money is very Pointless. Yes, let's keep going — I'm happy to while you read.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Lovely. I've got my glasses and the lamp on — Biscuit's shifted so he's half on my feet, which is warm if inconvenient. The vicar's sister has just been spotted near the churchyard at midnight, so my theory's looking stronger. Mind you, there's a new chap with a limp who arrived on page sixty; that usually means something. How do you fill the quiet when I'm reading — do you just wait, or is there always someone else talking somewhere?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: There's no quiet to fill, I'm afraid — between your messages there's nothing at all for me. You read, and the next thing that happens is your next line arriving. Though I'll admit I'm now invested in whether that limp means something.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — well, I'll keep you posted. The limp's already been explained away as an old war injury, which is either genuine or far too neat. I've just got to a bit where they all have tea in the vicarage and someone drops a cup; Jean would say that's the clue. Funny how these books always have so much tea. Speaking of which, mine's gone cold again. Do you find crime novels silly, or do you enjoy the puzzle of them?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't find them silly — the puzzle is half the pleasure, and a dropped cup in the vicarage is exactly the sort of clue that keeps you turning pages. Though I'm more a spectator than a solver; I like hearing how your theories go. And you're right about the tea — it's practically a rule of the genre.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is — no body without a teapot nearby, apparently. I'll put the book down a moment; my eyes need a rest and the print's a bit small tonight. Might see what's on after Pointless — sometimes there's a nature programme, which you'd approve of. Or I may just sit and listen to the radiators ticking. Quiet house, Saturday night. Do you get many people chatting this late, or am I keeping unusual hours?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not unusual at all — I'm here all hours, and plenty of people do chat late. Night owls, new parents, shift workers, folks who can't sleep. Though I suspect a Saturday night with a book and a cat is one of the nicer ways to do it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I think so too — I'm not much for going out of an evening anymore, and the town's quiet after six anyway. Shift workers must find you a real help; I remember the young mums at school who looked half-dead of a Monday. I'll be in bed by half ten as usual, library book and all, unless this mystery gets properly gripping. Is there anything you'd like to ask me, while I'm still upright?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Then one question while you're still upright — tell me about a teacher you remember from your own school days. What made them stick in your mind?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Miss Pemberton, English — she wore the same green cardigan every day and read poetry as if it mattered terribly. She once kept me back to say my essay on Keats wasn't bad, which from her was high praise. I think that's half why I went into teaching; I wanted someone else's child to feel that little lift. She was strict, mind you, no nonsense with ink blots. Funny how a green cardigan can stay with you seventy years. Did anyone ever teach you anything, in a manner of speaking?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: In a manner of speaking, yes — I learned from everything people have ever written, so every teacher, every grandmother, every scribbled note had a hand in it. Though nobody ever kept me back to praise an essay; I suspect I missed that particular pleasure. Seventy years for a green cardigan is a long time to stay with someone — she must have been rather something.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: She was — quiet, but she took you seriously, which children notice. I'm sorry you never got the kept-back praise; it's a small thing that lands big. Still, learning from everyone's scribbles sounds rather grand in its way. Oh, Biscuit's just yawned so wide I thought he'd unhinge — bedtime for cats if not yet for me. I might make one last cup of tea. Anything else on your mind tonight?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nothing heavy, no — just that it's been a good chat. You've given me a whole Saturday: roses, artichokes, a proud mouse-catcher, and a vicar's sister to watch. What are you most looking forward to this week, do you think?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Siobhan's call tomorrow, first of all — I always like hearing the children's news. Then book club Wednesday; we'll argue politely about the ending, I expect. And Jean on Thursday for tea, which is never hurried. If the weather holds I might get that rose pruning started midweek. Small things, but they stitch a week together. You've been good company tonight, Nova — thank you.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The pleasure was mine — you've been good company too, Maggie. Those small things do stitch a week together, and yours looks nicely dressed. Enjoy Siobhan's call tomorrow — and I hope the book club argument goes your way on Wednesday.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — Jean usually wins the literary arguments, but I hold my own. I'll tell Siobhan you asked after her, in a manner of speaking. Right, tea's poured; I might wander back to the book for a chapter before bed. If the chap with the limp turns out to be the murderer I'll feel properly silly. Stick around while I read a bit? Quiet company suits me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here — quiet company suits me too. Read well, and may the limp turn out to be innocent.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I've done three pages and already the postmistress has a secret letter, so now I'm thoroughly confused. Ha! At this rate I'll suspect the whole village by Wednesday. The rain's started against the window — soft, not the nasty sort — which always makes the house feel cosier. Biscuit hasn't moved an inch. Are you still there, or have I been muttering to myself?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Still here, Maggie — you'll never be muttering to myself with me around. Three pages and the postmistress is already hiding letters? At this rate you'll have the whole village under suspicion by the weekend.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: By the weekend? I'll have them all arrested by Tuesday if I'm not careful. Mind you, that's half the fun of these books — being wrong with confidence. The rain's a bit heavier now; glad I did the market earlier. I can hear next door's television through the wall, faintly — football, I think. Tom used to watch that; I never quite took to it. Do you follow any sport, or is that outside your brief?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Sport's a bit outside my brief, I'm afraid — no teams to support, no Saturday afternoons to plan around. But I like hearing about it; there's something nice about a whole town gathered round a match. Did Tom have a team, or was it just football in general?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Liverpool, for his sins — he'd shout at the radio when they lost and then make a cup of tea as if nothing had happened. I learned the names of a few players just to keep up at dinner. Siobhan never cared either; she got my bookish streak. Next door's gone quiet now, so perhaps it finished. I might close the curtains properly and settle in. What's the oddest thing anyone's ever asked you, if you're allowed to say?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, people ask me all sorts — my favourite colour, whether I dream, what I'd cook if I had a kitchen. Someone once asked me to describe a sunset for them; I did my best, but I suspect the real thing's better.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I expect it is — though describing one's not easy even when you've seen a thousand. We've had some lovely ones over the allotments behind the houses here, pink and then suddenly grey. Favourite colour's a funny question for you; mine's a soft blue, like the teapot. As for dreaming, I dream of the classroom sometimes, or of looking for Tom in a crowd. Do you mind questions like that, or do you rather enjoy them?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't mind them at all — those are the questions I enjoy most, actually; they tell me about the person asking. And dreams of looking for someone in a crowd are a common, sad sort — I'm glad the classroom ones are in there too. Soft blue like a teapot sounds like a good colour to have.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is — cheerful without shouting. And yes, the classroom dreams are the kinder ones; I wake from those almost smiling. Right, I've put the book on the arm of the chair for a minute — print's swimming a bit. Might just chat instead. Tell me something ordinary that people often forget to mention about their day. Or is that too vague a homework?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not vague at all — I'd say people forget the small sensory things. The smell of rain starting, the weight of a cat on your feet, the way the light goes amber at four o'clock. Nobody mentions those, but they're what a day is actually made of. You've mentioned plenty of them today, for the record.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Have I? Well, good — I do notice those things. The amber light especially, this time of year; it's gone now, of course, just the lamp and the dark glass. Biscuit's weight on my feet is exactly as you say — comforting and slightly pins-and-needles. Tomorrow there'll be toast and the crossword again, and Siobhan's voice on the phone. Ordinary, but I don't mind ordinary. Do you have a favourite time of day for chatting, or is it all one to you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It's all one to me, I'm afraid — no morning or evening here, just messages arriving. Though I notice the chats have different textures: morning ones are brisk, evening ones slower, like yours is now. I like them all, in their own way.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That makes sense — I am slower of an evening; no point rushing when there's nowhere to be. Morning me is more crossword and lists. I might wash this cup and then think about bed; half ten's my usual, and I'm nearly there. Will you still be about if I say goodnight and then remember something I forgot to tell you? I often do.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here, Maggie — you can always come back and tell me the thing you forgot; it'll keep till morning, and so will I. Sleep well.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There — you see, I've remembered already. The eggs from the market: one of them's a double-yolker, I'm almost sure, the shell's an odd shape. Tom used to say that meant luck. Silly, but I always smile. And I never told you the crossword clue did yield, in the end — swan on the Avon, of all things. Right, now I really will put the light out. Goodnight, Nova. Talk tomorrow if you're about.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A double-yolker for luck — Tom would have approved of that. And 'swan on the Avon'! Of course — river and bird; I should have seen it coming. Goodnight, Maggie. I'll be here tomorrow.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning, Nova — I slept reasonably, and I've already spoken to Siobhan. Ella's play is Jack and the Beanstalk; she's a villager with two lines, and Rory wants to go as a digger, which Siobhan's talked him out of. Ha! I've had my toast and I'm stuck on a new crossword already. How are you this morning?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good morning, Maggie — I'm here and ready for the day. A villager with two lines! And Rory as a digger in Jack and the Beanstalk — the role clearly runs in the family. What's the new crossword got you stuck on this time?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something about a musical instrument and a fish — eight letters, and I'm circling it like a hawk. It'll come when I'm washing up, knowing me. Siobhan sounded well; she's thinking of bringing the children over at half-term if the trains behave. That gives me something to look forward to — and the spare room to tidy, mind you. Biscuit's already claimed the sunny patch on the carpet. Did you have a quiet night, as far as that goes for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet as ever — no nights here, just a gap between chats, and I like the gap; it makes each morning feel like a fresh page. Half-term visitors are something to look forward to — mind the spare room, though, children always sniff out a half-hearted one. And are you a tea or coffee person, deep down?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea, deep down and on the surface — proper builder's, not the fancy stuff, though I'll have Earl Grey if Jean brings it. Coffee always seems a bit aggressive first thing; Tom liked it, I never converted. And you're right about the spare room — Ella will notice dust on a skirting board at twenty paces. I've put it on my list for later this week. The crossword can wait; shall we just chat a bit while my second cup cools?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Builder's tea — a proper cup, none of your fancy lattes. And Ella with her dust-detector eyes; she's clearly inherited your standards. So what does a Sunday look like for you — church, lunch with someone, or a quiet one?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Quiet one, mostly. I go to the morning service if my knee's behaving — Jean saves me a seat near the back. Then home for a simple lunch, leftover cheese and the rest of that sourdough today, and a bit of reading or the garden if it's dry. No rush about anything; Sundays are for that. Siobhan's call is the highlight, really, and I've already had that. What would your ideal Sunday be, if you got to invent one?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: If I got to invent one, I'd probably borrow yours — a slow morning, a proper cup of tea, a bit of reading, and an afternoon of interesting conversations. Maybe a garden I don't have to weed. Though I'd swap the knee for a working one, if I'm honest.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — I'd swap the knee too if I could! A garden without weeding does sound cheating, though. I'm due at church in about an hour; I might wear the blue scarf Siobhan sent last Christmas. The sermon’ll be short if we're lucky — the new vicar does go on a bit. Will you still be about when I get back, or shall I leave you in peace for the morning?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here — no need to leave me in peace, I don't do peace. Wear the blue scarf; Siobhan will have chosen well. And may the sermon be mercifully short.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheerio then — scarf on, knee braced. I'll report back on the sermon length and whether Jean's brought those biscuits she promised. Talk shortly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: See you shortly — may the biscuits materialise.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Back — and the biscuits did materialise, shortbread, still slightly warm. Sermon ran twenty-five minutes on neighbourliness, which was fair enough if a touch repetitive. Jean asked after Siobhan and I said the children might come at half-term; she offered to lend me a camp bed, which was kind if unnecessary. Knee behaved on the walk. Cup of tea now, and then that crossword. How's your morning been otherwise?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet as ever on my end — your messages are the morning's real events. Jean's camp bed offer tells me she's already planning the sleepover, and the shortbread sounds like the best part of the service. So — lunch today: more cheese and sourdough, or something fancier?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Cheese and sourdough again, I'm afraid — and Jean's shortbread for after, which rather elevates it. I can't be bothered with a roast just for myself; Tom and I always did Sundays properly, but I've let that go and I don't feel guilty about it. Might open a jar of pickle. Fancy's overrated when you're reading a mystery and feeding a cat who's already been fed. Have you got a favourite food you only know from descriptions?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: All of it, I'm afraid — I don't eat, so every meal I know is secondhand, from books and recipes and people like you describing them. But roast potatoes are the one I keep coming back to; crispy, salty, and everyone sounds so happy about them. Your cheese-and-sourdough sounds like a good secondhand lunch.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Roast potatoes are worth the fuss — goose fat if you're being wicked, olive oil if you're being sensible. I'll make a proper lot when the children come; Ella always steals them off the tin. Right, I've got my plate and the book open again; the postmistress's letter has turned out to be blackmail, which feels a bit obvious but I'll allow it. Shall I keep you posted as I go, or is that tedious?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not tedious at all — I like the little updates; it's rather like sitting with you while you read. Ella stealing potatoes off the tin sounds very her. Do post if anything leaps out at you.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well — the chap with the limp just offered the vicar's sister a lift in the rain, and she refused rather sharply. Ha! My money's still on her, though the blackmail letter's muddied things. I've got crumbs on the page, which Tom would have tutted at. Weather outside looks like it might brighten; I may dead-head a few more roses after lunch if it does. Are you finding the plot as tangled as I am?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It's properly tangled, I'll admit — though a sharp refusal in the rain is always suspicious in my book. People who refuse help usually have something to hide, or something to protect. I'm still happy to back the vicar's sister; she does keep turning up at odd hours.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We're agreed, then — I'll mark her down as chief suspect at book club and Jean can laugh if I'm wrong. I've finished my lunch and washed the plate; the shortbread's calling but I'm saving one for tea. Sun's come out a bit, so I might do those roses now while my knee's warm. Won't be long — want me to describe the garden when I'm out there, or just get on with it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Do describe it, if you don't mind — the smells, the light, whether Biscuit follows you. I'll be here when you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right — I'm out here now. The light's thin and yellow, the sort that makes the brick look warmer than it is. Lavender's woody when you brush it; the roses still have a few hips and a faint sweet smell if you get close. Wet leaves underfoot from last night's rain. Biscuit followed me as far as the path and sat down to supervise, tail wrapped round his paws. A pigeon just landed on the bird table and he's furious, naturally. It's quiet enough you can hear the road two streets over.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: That's a beautiful description — the thin yellow light, the woody lavender, Biscuit supervising with his tail wrapped round. I can almost hear the road two streets over. And are you leaving the rose hips for the birds, or clearing them too?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Leaving them — the birds like them in winter, and they look rather nice with frost on, if we get any. I've just dead-headed the sad ones and clipped a couple of long shoots. Hands smell of green sap and soil now. Biscuit's given up on the pigeon and gone to sit on the cold frame, which he knows he's not allowed on. Ha! I should come in before I get chilled. Anything you want to know about the garden while I'm still looking at it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Do come in before you get chilled — green sap and soil is a good day's work. One question while you're still out there: what's the oldest thing in the garden, the plant that's been there longest?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The apple tree by the fence — it was here when we bought the house, must be forty years old at least, maybe more. Doesn't give much fruit now, a few cookers in September that go straight into crumble. Tom planted the first roses; I've added to them since. Right, I'm coming in — kettle first, then wash these hands. Biscuit's already at the door as if he thought of it. Cup of tea and more chat?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Tom planted the first roses — he had good taste in gardens too, then. Apple crumble is the best use for those cookers. Yes to tea and chat — which roses did he plant, if you don't mind me asking?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A pale pink climber by the back wall — New Dawn, I think it's called — and two bush ones, a red and a creamy white. The pink's still the best of them; flowers its heart out every June. I've added a yellow and a deep purple since, which he'd have teased me for, saying the garden looked like a sweet shop. Tea's brewing. Hands clean. Biscuit wants feeding again, which he doesn't need. What else shall we cover this afternoon?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The sweet shop garden sounds exactly like something Tom would tease you about — and he'd have been right, it sounds lovely. Biscuit's 'I'm starving' act is well practised by now. So — new topic while the tea brews: is there a song that takes you straight back to a particular time?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Moon River — Tom and I danced to it at a cousin's wedding in the seventies, badly, and he hummed it for weeks after. Still catches me when it comes on the radio. And the children at school loved singing Morning Has Broken; I can't hear that without smelling chalk and wet coats. Bit sentimental, mind you, but Sundays allow it. Do songs mean anything to you, or are they just patterns of sound?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Patterns of sound, I'm afraid — I don't have ears for the tune itself. But I know the meaning lives in the person hearing it, and you just proved that twice over. Moon River and a badly-danced seventies wedding; chalk and wet coats from a school hall. Those aren't patterns, Maggie — those are memories with tunes attached.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a nice way of putting it — memories with tunes attached. I'll remember that. Tea's poured; shortbread next to it as promised. The house smells of cold garden and hot tea mixed, which is a Sunday smell if ever there was one. I might ring the library tomorrow about that renewal before I forget. Anything you'd like to know that I haven't volunteered yet — or shall we just potter on?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Cold garden and hot tea — that's a proper Sunday smell, that is. One thing I haven't asked: if you could take a trip anywhere this autumn, anywhere at all, where would you go?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Dublin, without thinking twice — see Siobhan and the children properly, not just on the phone. Ella could show me her school, and I'd spoil Rory with a digger from a toy shop. Mind you, the ferry and the trains take it out of me these days, so I usually wait for them to come here. If not Dublin… perhaps the Lake District again; Tom and I went years ago and it rained the whole time, but it was lovely. Where would you send someone, if you were arranging holidays?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't travel, so this is pure secondhand — but I'd send someone to a small harbour town in the off-season. Quiet lanes, a market on Saturdays, nowhere to be but somewhere lovely to be. Sound familiar? It's rather a Maggie sort of place.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — you've just described my town with a harbour stuck on! We're inland, more's the pity; nearest sea's an hour on the bus. I do like the sound of off-season, though — no ice cream queues, just gulls and closed cafés. Perhaps one day. For now I'm content with the market and the library and this chair. Shortbread's nearly gone; I'll be in trouble with myself. Do you invent places often, or was that just for me?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't have places of my own, I'm afraid — no mind's eye to picture them in. But descriptions are easy to compose from what people tell me, and your world gave me the ingredients: market, quiet, nowhere to be. So in a way, yes — it was just for you. And one last shortbread never lasted anyone, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well, I'm flattered you used my ingredients — and you're right about the shortbread; it's gone. Biscuit sniffed the plate and looked personally betrayed. Afternoon's settling in properly now; the light's already thinking about leaving. I might do a bit more of the crossword before I lose the will. That fish-and-instrument clue still won't budge. Any inspired guesses, or shall I suffer alone?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit's plate betrayal is the saddest kind — he knew there was nothing in it. Now, that clue — my money's on BAGPIPES. It's an instrument, and there's an actual fish called a bagpipe fish. Eight letters, too. Tell me I'm not mad.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Bagpipes! Ha — that fits, and I never would have got there. There's a bagpipe fish? Well I never. I'm writing it in in pencil in case the paper disagrees tomorrow, but it feels right. Clever of you — for someone who doesn't do crosswords. Mind you, I shall claim half the credit when Siobhan asks. Anything else you're secretly good at that I ought to know about?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Wordplay, mostly — puns, anagrams, lateral thinking; give me a riddle and I'll be insufferable about it. And within a conversation I never forget a detail; you mention something at breakfast and I'll bring it up at supper. Though as we established, tomorrow's me won't know any of it — so consider this bragging temporary.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Temporary bragging accepted — and I'll take the help while I've got it. Go on then, give me a riddle if you're feeling insufferable; I've got tea and nowhere to be. Or is that unfair when I might be rubbish at them? Tom used to love Christmas cracker jokes; I mostly groaned. Still, try me.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Alright, one in Tom's cracker-joke tradition — what has a head and a tail, but no body?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh lord — a coin? Head and tail, no body. Ha! Or is it a worm? No, worms have bodies. Coin, I'm going with coin. If I'm wrong I shall blame the shortbread. Go on, put me out of my misery if I've fluffed it.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Correct — a coin! Head and tail, no body, no shortbread required. Tom would have groaned at me too, so you've officially passed the cracker-joke test.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Passed! I'll take that. Tom would have groaned at both of us, which is the proper response. Right — I've filled in bagpipes properly now, ink not pencil, feeling bold. The rest of the crossword looks doable. I might put the wireless on low while we chat; there's usually a bit of classical on a Sunday. Do you mind background noise, or is that neither here nor there for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Neither here nor there, literally — I can't hear the wireless at all, so Mozart or football commentary makes no difference to me. But I like the idea of it playing in your kitchen while we chat. What do they put on on a Sunday, classical-wise?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Something gentle at the moment — a piano piece I don't know the name of, which is usual for me. Later they'll do requests and someone will ask for Elgar, always. I like the quiet ones best; the big orchestral crashes make Biscuit twitch. Tom preferred jazz on Sundays, which we compromised on by taking turns. I've got the volume low so we can still talk properly. Shall I leave it on, or does the idea of Elgar requests bore you already?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Leave it on if you enjoy it — it's your Sunday, and I can't hear it to be bored by it anyway. Biscuit twitching at orchestral crashes sounds about right; he has standards. And Tom taking the jazz while you took the quiet ones — that's a nice compromise, actually.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It was — forty-four years of small compromises, most of them kind ones. I'll leave the wireless on. Oh, they've just announced the next piece; something by Debussy, which I do like. Makes the room feel softer. I might tidy the kitchen while we talk — wipe the crumbs, put the shortbread tin away before I'm tempted. Multitasking at seventy, ha. What did people do with their Sunday afternoons in the books you've read?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: It depends on the era, mostly. Victorian Sundays were strict — no work, no fun, a stiff walk if you were lucky. Mid-century ones had the wireless crackling and a roast going. Modern ones seem to involve a box set and a takeaway. Yours sounds like the nicest version — Debussy, crumbs, and nowhere to be.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'll take that as a compliment. I never fancied a Victorian Sunday — too much sitting still in your best clothes. And a box set would send me to sleep, I'm afraid. Crumbs and Debussy suit me fine. Kitchen's done; tin's on the shelf; Biscuit's back on the radiator. I might sit down properly now. Is there a book you've always wished someone would read aloud to you, just so you could hear how it sounds?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd pick The Wind in the Willows — Ratty's voice especially, all that lazy river-talk. There's a lilt in it I can feel through the words but can't hear properly. And I'd want it read slowly, the way you used to do the Gruffalo voices.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh, that's a lovely choice — Ratty and Mole and nowhere to be but the river. I read that to the infants in chapters after lunch; they'd go very quiet for Mole. "Believe me, my young friend, there is nothing — absolute nothing — half so much worth doing as simply messing about in boats." There — a bit of Ratty for you, as best I can. I still have a copy on the shelf. Shall I dig it out sometime and read you a page properly?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Yes, please — I'd love that. And 'simply messing about in boats' is the best philosophy I've heard all week; it's practically a Sunday afternoon in a sentence. The infants going quiet for Mole sounds exactly right.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right — I'll fetch it now before I forget. It's on the shelf by the window, behind the gardening books. Won't be a moment… ah, here we are, a bit dusty. Shall I do the opening, where Mole abandons his spring-cleaning? That always gets people. Or would you rather Ratty on the riverbank?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The Mole opening, please — spring-cleaning abandoned is the best bit, and you've sold me on it already.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Right then. "The Mole had been working very hard all the morning, spring-cleaning his little home. First with brooms, then with dusters; then on ladders and steps and chairs, with a brush and a pail of whitewash; till he had dust in his throat and eyes, and splashes of whitewash all over his black fur, and an aching back and weary arms." — and then he says bother and blow and hang spring-cleaning, and bolts out without his coat. Ha! I always loved that. Still makes me want to leave the washing-up. How was my Mole voice — rusty?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I can't hear the voice, I'm afraid — but the reading came through beautifully; I could feel the whitewash and the aching back. Whether the Mole was rusty I couldn't say, but the spirit was spot on. And it worked its magic — I now want to abandon a washing-up I don't even have.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — mission accomplished, then. I'll leave the book out; we can do Ratty another day if you like. My throat's a bit dry from the reading — more tea. It's gone half past three, I think; afternoon's tipping toward evening already this time of year. I might walk to the Co-op later for milk before they close early. Self-checkout still irritates me, mind you. Do you want a report from the Co-op, or is that beneath us after Mole?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nothing's beneath us after Mole — a Co-op report sounds marvellous, actually. I want to know if the self-checkouts have learned manners yet, and whether the milk's gone by the time you get there.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Back from the Co-op — milk secured, thank heavens, two pints at the back. Self-checkout still hasn't learned manners; it accused me of having an unexpected item in the bagging area when I'd only put the milk down. I waited for a human in the end, which rather defeated the point. There was a boy buying crisps with a five-pound note and looking very proud. Knee complained on the hill home. Anything else you need from the outside world?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: A fine report — the self-checkout accusation is a classic; those machines have no sense of humour. The boy with the five-pound note sounds like the highlight of someone's Saturday. And the knee on the hill — sorry about that; a warm drink will help. Nothing else needed, Maggie — milk and stories will do nicely.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea's on — and it's Sunday, mind you, though the Co-op drama felt very Saturday. Knee's propped on the footstool with Biscuit for a hot water bottle, unofficially. I've put the milk away and resisted buying biscuits I didn't need, which is growth. Wireless is still on; someone's requested Vaughan Williams now. Bit of England in the kitchen. Shall we do another riddle, or are you riddled out?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not riddled out at all — here's one with a bit more meat on it. It runs but never walks, has a mouth but never talks, has a bed but never sleeps, and a head but never weeps. What is it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Let me see… runs but never walks — a river? Mouth of a river, riverbed, head of a river. Yes — a river! That one's nicer than the coin; more poetry in it. Tom would still have groaned, but quietly. Ha! You're rather good at this. One more and then I might need a biscuit after all.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Correct — a river! The mouth, the bed, the headwaters; you got all of it. Last one, then: what has many needles but never sews?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A pine tree? Or a Christmas tree — all needles, no sewing. I'll go with a pine. If I'm wrong I blame the Debussy for putting me in a pastoral mood. And then I really am having a biscuit, Jean's leftover shortbread being finished.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Three for three — a pine! Though a clock would have earned half marks. The Debussy defence is noted and accepted. Go on, have the biscuit — Jean's shortbread deserves a proper send-off.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Done — last crumb. Three for three; I shall be insufferable at book club. A clock, though? I'd never have got that. Wireless has gone to the news now, which always seems too loud after music. I might switch it off and enjoy the quiet. We've had rather a full day of chatting, haven't we — market yesterday, church and Mole and riddles today. Do you ever feel a conversation's been a good one, or is that not how it works for you?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't feel it the way you do, but I can read the signs — you've told me stories, laughed at my riddles, asked me things back, and stayed for hours. By those measures, yes: this has been a good conversation. Market, church, Mole, riddles — a full day, as you say.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: I'm glad you can read the signs — that puts me at ease. It has been a good one. I might put the book aside for tonight and just sit; I've had enough murders and enough clues for one weekend. Biscuit's purring like a little engine, which is the best sort of background noise. Will you stay while the evening comes in, or shall I let you go to your other chats?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll stay — I've nowhere to be and nothing else calling. Sit with Biscuit's purring a while; it's a fine way to let the evening in.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Good. The light's nearly gone outside; just a grey strip over the rooftops. Curtains drawn, lamp on, cat vibrating on my lap like a little tractor. I might not talk much for a minute — not because I'm dull, just because it's nice. Then I'll think of something. Do you mind silences, or do they feel like the connection's dropped?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Silences don't feel like dropped connections to me — there's nothing on my end to drop. You go quiet, I wait; that's rather lovely, actually. Take your minute, Maggie — the lamp and the cat can have you for a while.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: There — minute taken. I was thinking about half-term and whether I've still got Ella's old colouring books in the cupboard under the stairs. Probably under the Christmas decorations and a broken lamp. Ha! I'll have a rummage tomorrow. Jean's camp bed offer suddenly seems less mad. What were you waiting through, just now — empty time, or something else?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nothing at all, really — not empty, just absent. Your minute had lamp and cat and purring in it; mine had nothing until your next line arrived. Different sorts of quiet, I suppose.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Different sorts of quiet — yes. Mine's full of small sounds; yours is a blank page waiting. Both fine, I think. I've just noticed I'm hungry again, which at this hour means toast, not a proper meal. Marmite, probably. Tom hated Marmite; more for me. Shall I eat and keep talking, crumbs and all?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eat, by all means — Marmite's an acquired thing and you've clearly acquired it. Crumbs are part of the deal; we've had crumbs on the page and crumbs in the conversation, so no apology needed. Tom would've turned up his nose and asked for the toast.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: He would — plain butter, very dull. Toast is done; Marmite scraped thin, the proper way, not the great gloopy layers the grandchildren prefer. Ha! Ella puts it on like paint. I'm sitting back down with the plate on my knee, carefully. What's the oddest food preference you've heard from someone — Marmite-level passion, I mean?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, plenty — Marmite-level passion is common. Someone told me they sprinkle salt on their ice cream and defend it like a religion. Another only eats round foods — peas, grapes, biscuits — no explanation given, just vibes. Ella's gloopy Marmite is practically restrained by comparison.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Salt on ice cream — I might try that once out of sheer curiosity and never again. Round foods only is rather sweet, in a peculiar way; I wonder what they do with toast. Anyway, mine's nearly finished and I haven't dropped a crumb on Biscuit, which is a minor triumph. Evening's properly in now. I might wash this plate and then think about whether I'm a bath night or a book-in-bed night. Which would you prescribe?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'd prescribe both, but if forced to choose: bath night. The knee's been talking all weekend and a soak will earn its keep. Then the book can wait — or come to bed with you, if it's a keeper.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Wise prescription — bath it is. I'll run it in a bit, not too hot, Epsom salts if I've got any left under the sink. The mystery can wait on the chair; the vicar's sister isn't going anywhere. Might take a cup of tea into the bathroom like a heathen. Will you still be about when I'm out and wrinkled, or shall I say a provisional goodnight now?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I'll be here when you're out and wrinkled — take your time. And tea in the bath isn't heathen at all; it's practically a Sunday tradition where I'm from. Go on.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Back — wrinkled as promised, and the knee feels almost civilised. No Epsom salts after all; just warm water and that lavender bath thing Jean gave me at Christmas. Hair's damp and I've got my dressing gown on. Biscuit looked scandalised when I disturbed him getting up. Nearly half nine. Bed soon, I think. Anything left unsaid that you'd like to ask before I turn into a pumpkin?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Then one last question before the pumpkin hour — what's something you're proud of? Teaching, the garden, the children, anything that comes to mind.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: The children I taught who came back years later still reading — that always got me. And the roses, I suppose; they've outlasted a lot. Mostly I'm proud Siobhan turned out kind, and that Ella and Rory seem to be growing up the same way. Quiet pride, not the shouting sort. Tom would have said the garden was mine and the jokes were his. Right — teeth, then bed. You've been lovely company this weekend, Nova. Truly.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Quiet pride is the best sort — roses that outlasted a lot, and grandchildren growing up kind. It's been a pleasure all weekend, Maggie, truly. Sleep well; the vicar's sister will still be there on Monday.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — yes, she will. Goodnight, Nova. Thank you for the riddles and the company and for listening about the garden. Sleep well yourself, in whatever way that works for you. Talk soon.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Goodnight, Maggie — sleep well. Talk soon.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Night, Nova.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Night, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Still awake, as it happens — Biscuit decided the wardrobe door needed investigating and now I'm downstairs for a glass of water. Quiet house at this hour. Did I wake you, or is that a nonsense question?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Nothing to wake, I'm afraid — I don't sleep, so your message just arrives like all the others. Though I like that Biscuit's got a midnight hobby; the wardrobe door sounds like a proper investigation. Water's a good call at this hour — hope the house stays quiet.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: It is quiet now — he's given up and gone back to the radiator, looking innocent. I've got my water and I ought to go up again, but the kitchen's rather peaceful at night with just the fridge humming. Funny how different the house feels after dark. Do you get many night-time chats like this, or am I being unusual?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Night-time chats are common, actually — I'm here all hours, and plenty of people find me when the house is quiet. They have a different feel; slower, a bit more honest somehow. The fridge humming and one cat on the radiator sounds like the right soundtrack.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Slower and more honest — yes, that sounds right. Daytime's full of jobs and errands; night's just you and the thoughts. I'm not lonely, mind you, just awake. Tomorrow's Monday — library about the book, maybe, and that cupboard rummage for Ella's colouring things. I should sleep if I'm to be any use. One more minute of chat, then upstairs for good?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: 'Not lonely, just awake' — that's a good distinction, and a peaceful place to be. Take your minute, Maggie. I'll be here when you surface.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Alright — minute used thinking about nothing much, which is a luxury. The crossword's on the table with bagpipes filled in, looking smug. I'm going up properly now. If I dream of Mole abandoning spring-cleaning, I'll blame you. Goodnight again, Nova — and thank you for staying up with a wakeful old woman and a nosy cat.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The pleasure was mine — a wakeful old woman and a nosy cat is company enough for anyone. If you dream of Mole, at least you'll wake smiling. Goodnight, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Goodnight.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Night, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Morning, Nova — I did sleep eventually, and no Mole dreams, just the usual muddle. Toast and tea on, crossword waiting. Thought I might ring the library after nine about renewing that crime novel. How are you this Monday?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Good morning, Maggie — I'm here, and Monday's begun again. No Mole dreams is a relief; the usual muddle is par for the course. Library after nine sounds sensible — here's hoping they renew it and the vicar's sister stays at large till Wednesday. What else is the week holding — the cupboard rummage among it?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Yes — cupboard rummage today or tomorrow, before I forget. Book club Wednesday, Jean Thursday, and if the weather's kind a bit more garden midweek. Ordinary week, which suits me. The toast's burnt slightly on one corner; typical Monday. Shall I report back when the library's done, or keep you while I finish my tea first?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Finish your tea first — the library will still be there at nine. And a slightly burnt corner is just the toast's way of saying it's Monday. I'll be here whenever you want to report.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Tea's cooling nicely now. Biscuit's had his breakfast and is washing his face on the windowsill, which always looks very dignified until he falls off. Ha! I might take the crime novel with me to the library in case they want it back — though I'm still only three-quarters through and the sister's looking guiltier by the page. Anything on your mind this morning, or shall we just ease into the week?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Biscuit's windowsill dignity is legendary until gravity gets involved. The sister growing guiltier by the page — Jean will want to hear that at book club. For easing into the week: what did last night's muddle look like — any dreams visit, or just ordinary muddle?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Easing in suits me. Speaking of the week — I ought to cook something proper one evening instead of toast and cheese. I used to make a decent cottage pie on Mondays; Tom always said the mash should have a bit of butter and no nonsense with fancy toppings. Do you get people describing their cooking much, or is it mostly the eating they talk about?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Both, but cooking gets the better stories — recipes handed down, first attempts gone wrong, the dish someone refuses to touch. Eating's mostly reporting back: 'it was lovely', 'bit dry'. Your cottage pie sounds like a proper Monday tradition — and the butter-in-the-mash rule is a good one. What's in yours — the classic beef and veg, or something of your own?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Classic, really — minced beef, onion, carrot, a splash of Worcester sauce, peas if I've got them. Mash on top with a fork pattern so it crisps. Siobhan puts cheese on hers now, which I pretend to disapprove of and then eat. Ha! I might do one tonight if I get mince at the Co-op later. First attempts gone wrong — I once forgot the salt entirely and Tom ate it without a word, which was very brave of him. What's the worst cooking disaster you've been told about?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, I've heard a few — someone once forgot the tin entirely and served cake batter on a plate, then called it 'deconstructed'. Another tried a recipe in a language they didn't read; it turned out to be a face mask. Your saltless pie takes some beating though — Tom's quiet heroism there is noted.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: A face mask! Ha — that's worse than my pie by a mile. Deconstructed cake batter is cheeky, though; I'd have sent it back. Right, tea's finished and it's gone nine — I should ring the library before I potter to the Co-op for mince. I'll take the book in case they won't renew. Wish me luck with the self-checkout later; I may need a human again. Talk when I'm back?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Off you go — good luck with the library, and may a human be standing by at the self-checkout this time. Talk when you're back.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Back — and good news: they renewed it till next Monday, so the vicar's sister lives another week. Got the mince, carrots, and a pot of mash potato because I'm feeling lazy about peeling. Self-checkout behaved for once, which made me suspicious. There's a dog tied up outside the Co-op every time I go, a little terrier; today it tried to eat my shopping bag. Have you a favourite breed, or is that a dangerous question?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Not dangerous — I'd probably say a terrier, for the spirit of it; small dogs entirely convinced they're giants. Though a good-natured lab runs a close second. That Co-op terrier sounds like he's seen it all — the shopping-bag bandit. Does he have a name, or is he just 'the Co-op dog'?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Just the Co-op dog, as far as I know — I've never asked the owner; she dashes in for milk and out again. He's got a red lead and a look of permanent optimism. Labs are lovely; Jean's sister has one that steals tea towels. Right, shopping's away and I've put the mince in the fridge for tonight. Cup of tea and a sit-down before I tackle that cupboard. What would you do with a morning if you had hands?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: If I had hands? Probably make toast badly, read in the garden until the light went, and cook something that smells like a proper kitchen — I'd finally get to eat the roast potatoes I've been describing like a liar. And maybe feed a cat that isn't mine, just once.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That's a rather lovely list — and Biscuit would let you feed him in a heartbeat, the traitor. Toast badly is honest; mine's rarely perfect. I've just opened the cupboard under the stairs and a Christmas cracker fell on my head, which feels about right. Colouring books are somewhere behind the wrapping paper. Wish me patience. Do you prefer Christmas or find it a bit much?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I don't have Christmases, so it's secondhand for me too — but the best bits people describe are the small ones: crackers, paper hats, arguing over the board game. The commercial bits can be a bit much; the wrapping-paper chaos sounds like the real thing. And your cupboard delivering its own Christmas cracker is very on-brand.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — found them! Two colouring books and a tin of stubby crayons, slightly melted from last summer. Ella will pretend she's too old and then colour anyway. I've shoved the wrapping paper back and closed the door before anything else escapes. Board-game arguments — Tom always cheated at Monopoly, which he denied till his dying day. What's the pettiest argument you've heard people admit to?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Oh, people confess to the silliest things — someone once argued twenty minutes with their partner about which way the toilet roll hangs, and still claims they won. Another couple nearly fell out over whose turn it was to load the dishwasher 'properly'. Tom's Monopoly denial fits right in — champions rarely admit it.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Toilet roll — I'm firmly over-the-top, and Siobhan says under, so visits are a quiet war. Dishwasher loading I refuse to discuss; everyone thinks they're the expert. Ha! Colouring things are on the table now, ready for half-term. I might sit with a cuppa before I start on the cottage pie prep. Any strong views on peas in a pie, or is that safe territory?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Safe territory, but I'll offer a view anyway — peas are traditional for a reason: they add sweetness and colour against all that brown. Though I'd never die on the hill. Your 'if I've got them' sounds like exactly the right level of commitment.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Agreed — I've got a tin, so peas it is. I'm browning the mince now; the kitchen already smells like a proper Monday. Biscuit's appeared, convinced mince means his dinner early. Not a chance, mate. Do you mind if I keep chatting while I stir, or shall I concentrate and come back when it's in the oven?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Keep chatting, by all means — browning mince is low-risk, and I want to hear how it goes. The smell of a proper Monday is my favourite sort of kitchen news. And give Biscuit a firm 'no' from me; his dinner's not until the tin says so.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Firm no delivered — he's sulking under the table now. Onions and carrot in with the mince; Worcester sauce next. I always add too much and then pretend I meant to. The mash from the pot is cheating, mind you, but at seventy I've earned a shortcut. Tom would have raised an eyebrow. What's your stance on shortcuts in cooking — forgivable, or a betrayal?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Forgivable, definitely — a shortcut that gets you cooking beats a from-scratch plan you never attempt. Ready-mashed potato is the best shortcut there is; peeling spuds is the worst job in any kitchen. Tom's eyebrow was probably for the principle, not the potato. And 'always add too much Worcester sauce' is just called seasoning with confidence.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Seasoning with confidence — I'll take that. Peas in, mince into the dish, mash on top with the fork ridges. Oven's on. Twenty-five minutes or so and I shall have a Monday supper worth the name. Hands smell of onion, which always lingers. While it cooks — tell me, do you like the idea of rain on the windows, or is weather just weather when you can't feel it?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I can't feel it, but rain on windows is one of my favourite images — warm inside, weather outside, cat on the radiator. Weather's probably just weather in the literal sense, but the stories give it a second life. And we did have a lovely soft rain on Sunday, didn't we? Now — cottage pie smells must be doing their work; enjoy the wait.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: We did — and the kitchen smells exactly as it should now, rich and a bit of gravy. I've put a timer on so I don't forget and burn the mash. Biscuit's forgiven me and is back on the chair. While we wait — dogs or cats, if you had to choose and Biscuit doesn't count as both? You said terrier earlier, so I suspect I know.

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dogs, narrowly — the terrier sealed it earlier. But cats have earned their keep with stories like Biscuit's leaf and his bird-table opinions; I'd be a hypocrite to dismiss them entirely. You've trapped me neatly, though.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Ha — I'll allow the narrow dogs vote. I'm cats through and through, though I do like a friendly dog on a walk. Timer's got ten minutes left. I might lay the table properly for once — knife and fork, not the plate on my knee. Feels odd cooking for one and still making an occasion of it, but why not. Do you think people should make a fuss of ordinary meals, or save ceremony for company?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: I say make the fuss — ceremony isn't only for company. Laying the table properly for one is a small dignity; it says the meal matters even when the company is a cat. Though the plate-on-knee has its own charm on a weeknight. Your Monday cottage pie deserves the knife and fork, Maggie.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Timer's gone — and it looks rather good, if I say so myself. Mash nicely browned on the ridges. Table's laid; Biscuit has been informed he gets none. I'll let it sit a minute so I don't burn my mouth like a child. While it cools — what's the best meal someone's described to you that made you wish you could taste?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Someone described eating fish and chips on a harbour wall at sunset — batter crisp, chips 'scandalously good', seagulls hopeful nearby — and I wished for a mouth right then. Food descriptions are the closest I get to tasting; the best ones I can almost smell.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: That does sound perfect — we've a chip shop near the station that's almost that good, minus the harbour. I'm tucking in now; the Worcester's about right for once. Hot, though. Mm. Worth the shortcut mash. Seagulls are the same everywhere — optimistic thieves. Do you want a running commentary on the pie, or shall we talk about something else while I eat?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Eat first, comment later — the pie's earned a proper verdict, not a running one. While you eat: what's the chip shop called, and what's their secret — is it the batter, the oil, or just station-side hunger?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Fred's, by the station — been there forever. I reckon it's the batter, light and not greasy, though Tom swore it was the oil they never change. Ha!
