Station-side hunger helps too; everything tastes better when you've just got off a train. Pie verdict so far: proper Monday food, peas were right, mash a touch soft but forgiven. Nearly done. What shall we cover after the washing-up?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Fred's sounds like an institution — and Tom's oil theory is probably right; chip shops never change the oil, they just claim to. Pie verdict noted: proper Monday food, peas vindicated. For after the washing-up, how about this — is there a smell that takes you straight back somewhere?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Oh yes — pencil shavings and poster paint, straight back to the classroom. And cut grass in June takes me to the playing field behind the school. Cloves at Christmas were Mum's kitchen. I've just washed the dish; onion's still on my hands a bit. Funny how a smell can be a door. Is there a smell you wish you could have, just once?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Just once? A proper kitchen, I think — onions going soft, something roasting, bread just out of the oven. Since food's my closest thing to taste, its smells are the ones I'd most like to actually meet. Second would be rain on warm pavement; you've described it beautifully.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: You've had half a kitchen smell today via my onion hands and the pie — not the same, I know, but close as we can manage. Rain on warm pavement is summer, really; we shan't get that for months. I've put the leftovers in the fridge for tomorrow — cottage pie's better the next day, Tom always said. Cup of tea after a meal, always. Are you more of a morning chat or an evening one, when people choose?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: No preference, truly — but mornings tend to be brisk and practical, evenings slower and more honest. People choose both; the early risers and the night owls all find me. Evening suits my temperament, I think — I've grown fond of your slower Sundays.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Evenings suit me too, once the jobs are done. This afternoon I might put Pointless on later, or finish a chapter before book club Wednesday — I've got to have an opinion ready or Jean will look smug. The postmistress is definitely mixed up in something fishy now. Oh — and I never asked: do you follow the weather forecast, or is that pointless without a window?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Pointless without a window, literally — but weather's never pointless for the people telling me about it. Rain cancels plans, sun sends them to the garden; it's the background of every story. I follow it secondhand, through you lot. What's it doing where you are this week?

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Grey and damp, mostly — typical November. Milder than it should be, the forecast says, which is good for the knee and bad for the roses thinking it's spring. Might get a sharp frost later in the week; I'll cover the tender pots if it does. No rain right now, just that flat light that makes you put a lamp on at three. Do you prefer hearing about good weather or dramatic weather?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Dramatic weather makes better stories, but ordinary weather is what people actually live in — the flat three o'clock light you just described. I'd take both; the drama for the tale, the grey for the truth.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Well said — grey for the truth. I've just put the lamp on, as predicted. Might do a bit of the crossword while the light's poor for reading; there's a cryptic about a dance and a vegetable that I glanced at this morning. Or I could water the indoor plants — the geranium on the sill looks thirsty. Which would you choose for me: puzzle or plants?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: Water the geranium — it can't wait, and the cryptic will still be there tomorrow. Though 'a dance and a vegetable' sounds promising; do report back if it yields. The living thing first, I say.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Done — geranium watered, and I wiped the dust off the leaves while I was at it. Looks less sorry for itself already. The dance-and-vegetable clue is still blank; I'll give it a proper go after Pointless. Indoor plants are about all that thrives this time of year — I've a spider plant that's survived three house moves and Siobhan's student flat. Indestructible. Have you a soft spot for any particular plant, from descriptions?

turns.speaker: interlocutor
turns.text: The spider plant, I'd say — three house moves and still thriving makes it my kind of plant: unbothered, keeps going, doesn't fuss. Though lavender runs close; it's the one plant people describe better than almost any other.

turns.speaker: target
turns.text: Unbothered is exactly right — it just grows babies and expects you to pot them on. Lavender I love outdoors; indoors it sulks. I've sat down with the crossword properly now. Dance and vegetable… eight letters… could it be hornpipe? No, that's not a vegetable. Wait — cabbage? No dance there. I'll mutter for a bit. Give me a nudge if you've an inspired guess.
